title: Patagonia's Founder Urged Fewer Pitons. Did He Dare in 1973? | Brand Story
description:
How does a man who sells pitons persuade climbers to use the hammer less? Follow Chouinard's hand-forged products, a 1970 reply and the 1972 catalog to the opening moves of his 1973 ascent of El Capitan's Nose with Bruce Carson. An added original first-person account preserves details of chocks moving, a partner's doubts and their subsequent progress.

Carson's article was published in 1974; the events it recounts took place in 1973. The year 1977 is only the publication year of a separate interview article, not a confirmed date for the visit. Historical scenes use anonymous conceptual illustrations; they do not reconstruct real people's appearances or actual climbing routes, or provide climbing instructions.

chapters.c09r5-shot-009: First, He Taught You to Trust That Piton
chapters.c09r5-shot-028: The Other Cost of a Handy Tool
chapters.c09r5-shot-049: Fourteen Pages to Change One Habit
chapters.c09r5-shot-086: The Seller Puts His Weight on a Chock

c09r5001.text: A skilled climbing team can place and retrieve a hundred pitons in a day. You might be the next person to climb that crack.

c09r5002.text: The pitons are gone, but the scars from hammering may still be there in front of you.

c09r5003.text: Open a 1972 equipment catalog and set a steel piton beside it.

c09r5004.text: Chouinard, who would later found Patagonia, was urging customers to show restraint with equipment in his own catalog.

c09r5005.text: That's an odd position: he still had gear to sell, but an old habit needed to change.

c09r5006.text: What I most want to see is what he would pack when he stood beneath a big wall himself.

c09r5007.text: This time, we'll follow the Patagonia founder's advice to an ascent where it actually had to bear weight.

c09r5008.text: What can a man who sells pitons do to convince you that you can use the hammer less?

c09r5009.text: That advice first had to get past the pitons Chouinard himself had sold. Let's turn the clock back to 1957.

c09r5010.text: He later told a reporter that almost nobody in America was making pitons then, and an earlier blacksmith's gear was no longer available.

c09r5011.text: Early soft-iron pitons deformed to fit cracks and weren't intended for repeated use. A long route meant carrying dozens of them.

c09r5012.text: The earlier maker had used steel from car front axles. That rigid material took pitons down a different path from soft iron.

c09r5013.text: His hard-steel pitons could be pulled out and used again. After one section of a climb, the gear could keep going with you.

c09r5014.text: What would you do if you couldn't buy suitable equipment: wait for someone to restock it, or make it yourself?

c09r5015.text: Chouinard bought a small coal forge, an anvil and tongs, learned forging from books, and began making pitons from chrome-molybdenum steel.

c09r5016.text: He loaded his tools into a car and traveled along the California coast. He'd stop for a day or two, fire up the forge, make a batch and sell it at climbing areas.

c09r5017.text: How many pitons could this traveling workshop turn out in an hour?

c09r5018.text: By his recollection, just two. Sometimes he spent eight hours a day at the forge.

c09r5019.text: What interests me is that something made so slowly still had to get buyers to open their wallets. What did it cost?

c09r5020.text: He said European pitons were about thirty cents each then, while each of his was priced at a dollar fifty. Many people initially thought that was expensive.

c09r5021.text: He also recalled that it took several years for customers to gradually accept that his pitons were worth the price.

c09r5022.text: In summer, he sold at climbing areas. In winter, he made stock for the following summer.

c09r5023.text: Once customers were ordering by mail instead of standing in front of him, could deliveries keep that same rhythm?

c09r5024.text: In 1964, the first mail-order catalog was just a mimeographed price list. It even warned against expecting prompt delivery from May through September.

c09r5025.text: But as orders grew, could he keep up by forging every piton by hand?

c09r5026.text: Production later brought in machines and dies. A partner who had studied aeronautical engineering also helped design manufacturing tools.

c09r5027.text: The gear became available and more people began using it. Getting customers to put it aside, though, meant more than putting a different product in their gear bags.

c09r5028.text: By 1967, an equipment article by Chouinard and his partner had set out a whole sequence of actions around the piton.

c09r5029.text: The article described placing a piton, attaching a carabiner and aid ladder, testing it with body weight, then moving up. The piton wasn't just protection after you'd moved past it.

c09r5030.text: The article called for a consistent sequence at every piton, avoiding unnecessary rope handling to save time and effort while moving the body.

c09r5031.text: In this kind of aid climbing, climbers put their weight on the gear. Even an overnight hammock could hang from pitons.

c09r5032.text: If you entrusted your body to a small piece of metal, would you instinctively think that hammering it deeper made it safer?

c09r5033.text: Yet the article called driving pitons too deep the most common mistake. In a vertical crack, a piton also had to resist rotation.

c09r5034.text: It asked climbers to find a suitable crack that would naturally grip the piton, rather than simply pound away at its head.

c09r5035.text: And who else would have to deal with the consequences of that extra hammer blow?

c09r5036.text: The person removing the piton later. The article said to count both placement and removal time: one extra blow could make retrieval harder.

c09r5038.text: What I want to know is whether the seller who knew those movements so well was ready to change himself.

c09r5039.text: A later interview quoted a reply he wrote in 1970: Chouinard said chocks were useful, but he wouldn't normally use them instead of pitons.

c09r5040.text: He even complained that a partner who insisted on chocks took much longer placing gear than he would have spent hammering in pitons.

c09r5041.text: But as his hands grew more accustomed to the hammer, could those cracks keep taking it forever?

c09r5043.text: Back to the scars in our opening: the catalog explained the cause plainly. Granite was softer than alloy-steel pitons, and hammering them in and out loosened flakes of rock.

c09r5044.text: You could take that piton in your pack back home, but the crack had widened. What could the next climber place there?

c09r5045.text: The report said some cracks that once took small pitons later needed larger ones.

c09r5046.text: Chouinard had initially thought climbing didn't harm rock. He later acknowledged that it could do great damage.

c09r5047.text: If he wanted people to change that action, would simply selling one more kind of gear be enough?

c09r5049.text: The chocks he proposed weren't a new invention that year. British climbers had long been wedging objects into cracks.

c09r5050.text: From small stones to metal nuts with holes, rope could go around or through them to connect them to the climber.

c09r5051.text: Chocks lodge in cracks because of their shape and can usually be retrieved later. What they remove is the process of hammering pitons in and hammering them out again.

c09r5052.text: You might ask: knowing that less hammering is good is one thing, but how do you get this unfamiliar piece of gear to stay put?

c09r5053.text: The catalog commissioned a specialist article from a climbing writer. The later interview said those instructions ran to fourteen pages.

c09r5054.text: Sometimes one chock wasn't enough: two or more had to work together. But how could several placements form one system?

c09r5055.text: The interview compared those connected placements to a bridge truss: several positions working together to strengthen the whole connection.

c09r5056.text: The original said this approach required a closer relationship with the rock. To me, reading the crack in front of you is the difficult part.

c09r5057.text: But after reading those pages, could anyone demand that you make the same choice in every crack?

c09r5058.text: The foreword first said not to add pitons on routes already climbed without them. On other suitable routes, removable chocks should be considered first.

c09r5059.text: Where pitons really were necessary, the foreword proposed leaving them fixed, reducing repeated hammering and removal. But how would later climbers know?

c09r5060.text: Their locations also had to be recorded in the local climbing guide.

c09r5061.text: Would those choices actually make a difference to the rock, or did they just sound good on paper?

c09r5062.text: The foreword pointed to old British routes: the footholds were already polished, but protection cracks that hadn't been hammered with pitons remained intact.

c09r5063.text: The catalog also changed the measure of success: not just whether you reached the top, but how you got there.

c09r5064.text: But when you turned to the products and prices, might you ask: what gives this seller the right to tell me how to climb?

c09r5065.text: A 1973 review treated the seventy-two-page product catalog as a book. Some people felt their freedom as climbers was at stake.

c09r5066.text: They said the people most insistent on switching to chocks had already climbed those big walls with pitons, and were only now asking those who came after to change methods.

c09r5067.text: Those critics doubted that the long routes could be completed without pitons. If they accepted this ethic, they would lose their chance.

c09r5068.text: My question is whether Chouinard, who was making that demand, could himself complete a big-wall route with chocks.

c09r5069.text: The resistance didn't only come from younger climbers. A piece written by an older climber circulated widely on the East Coast.

c09r5070.text: Its author mocked the idea of paying for a catalog only to read about gear he couldn't afford and receive sermons he didn't need.

c09r5074.text: The reviewer of the catalog also noticed that in Yosemite he was meeting more people determined to climb without hammers or pitons.

c09r5075.text: Some were already willing to try. Who would that seller team up with to tackle a longer route?

c09r5076.text: Carson, who would later become his partner, wrote in a May 1973 letter about an attempt without a hammer.

c09r5077.text: That route required rappelling down to the start. If they couldn't climb back out through the first five pitches, they'd have to cross a river to leave.

c09r5078.text: If you were already down there, would leaving out the hammer still be just a small difference in your pack?

c09r5079.text: He persuaded another partner to try. They climbed from morning until sunset, avoiding fixed pitons but still using existing bolts.

c09r5080.text: Carson wrote that without a hammer sling in the way, there was also less temptation to give a chock a quick tap and force it in.

c09r5081.text: The next day, though, a horizontal crack left him with a problem: the chocks could only be placed in one direction.

c09r5082.text: Remember the catalog's explanation of combining several placements? What did Carson actually do this time?

c09r5083.text: He first paired two pieces in opposing directions, then linked the later placements all the way back to that initial point.

c09r5084.text: Over the following months, he completed more clean climbs. Only after that experience built up did he feel ready to try a longer route.

c09r5086.text: In late August 1973, Carson and Chouinard discussed aid climbing with chocks and agreed to go to Yosemite together.

c09r5087.text: Their objective was the Nose route on El Capitan.

c09r5088.text: The gear bag from our opening held no pitons this time: chocks took their place. Ropes and other climbing equipment still went up the wall with them.

c09r5089.text: The account appeared in the following year's American Alpine Journal, written by Carson himself. Two weeks after making their plans, Chouinard went up first.

c09r5090.text: Would you expect the gear he'd personally recommended to stay exactly where he put it as soon as it took weight?

c09r5091.text: Carson wrote that when Chouinard put his weight on the first chock, it sank about a quarter of an inch, roughly six millimeters.

c09r5092.text: Then the second chock also moved when it took his weight.

c09r5093.text: The two had never climbed together before. Watching those first two moves, what went through Carson's mind?

c09r5094.text: He wrote that his heart sank. He even began considering setting off the next morning with his solo gear if that day came to nothing.

c09r5095.text: Chouinard continued working through thin cracks, using several small pieces on the first pitch. Following and retrieving the gear, Carson began to see the difficulty of those placements.

c09r5097.text: I want to know: did Carson really end up leaving his partner and following through on the solo plan he'd considered?

c09r5098.text: No. Three pitches later, he wrote, the two were working smoothly and efficiently together, and his thoughts of soloing had disappeared.

c09r5099.text: Placing chocks on the first four pitches took considerable work. At the ledge, they rappelled down at sunset.

c09r5100.text: The wall above was still waiting. Would leaving the hammer behind make the entire ascent this slow?

c09r5101.text: Carson recorded that as they continued upward, the chocks became easier to place, and the two climbed faster.

c09r5102.text: Aid climbing alternated with climbing natural cracks. They traveled light, and hauling their supplies caused no problems.

c09r5103.text: Two sections higher up still slowed them down. Chouinard led one difficult passage, and another section also needed careful handling.

c09r5104.text: After such an awkward start, would even their supplies become a problem by the end?

c09r5105.text: They moved faster than planned and still had plenty of water. Both overnight stops had suitable ledges, so they could stop early and watch the sunset.

c09r5106.text: They completed the ascent over several days. Carson described it as one of his most satisfying climbs involving several days on a wall.

c09r5107.text: But might one successful partnership just have been a matter of those two particular climbers?

c09r5108.text: In autumn 1973, another team of three completed a clean ascent of the Nose, reporting no particularly difficult chock placements.

c09r5109.text: For Carson, leaving the hammer at home brought back the unknown, even for climbers who already knew big walls well.

c09r5111.text: Would you trust a seller more if they openly shared the difficulties they encountered while using the product? Let me know in the comments.

c09r5112.text: Subscribe to see how familiar brands' claims stand up to actual use.
